messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rafael is a 62-year-old married Latino man who has spent most of his adult life as a dancer, and he still teaches and rehearses in a studio where bodies move close together and touch is part of the work. The collision happened late one evening as he was driving home after class. Another car ran a light and struck the driver’s side hard enough to spin his vehicle. What has stayed with him is not a clear story but fragments that come back with force: the explosive crash of metal, the shriek of brakes, a horn blaring somewhere too long, and the sensation that events had outrun his ability to act. When he tries to describe it, he stalls out and says it is “like noise and impact, not words.” In those moments of recall he feels a wave of shame that is hard for him to explain, as if there is something humiliating in having been so exposed and overpowered.

In the months after the crash, Rafael found that entering any room had become a quiet tactical exercise. At the studio, before he could focus on music or choreography, he was already noting the exits, the door to the hall, the back stairwell, who was standing where. If a student came up behind him and touched his shoulder unexpectedly, he jerked violently and felt a surge of alarm out of proportion to the moment. He was often flooded with fear, anger, and shame afterward. He had come to believe that bad things could happen without warning and that he was the kind of person they happened to. That sense of helplessness and character-based blame made every space feel less safe; scanning for ways out and bracing against sudden contact felt necessary, not excessive.

The heightened vigilance also seemed to sharpen the way the crash returned to him. When he was already on edge in rehearsal, a squeal from the sound system or the scrape of a chair could bring back the sound of the collision in his head with startling immediacy. The memory did not come as a coherent narrative but as auditory fragments and bodily shock, leaving him tense and ashamed before he had fully registered why. He noticed that the more keyed up he was—watching doors, flinching at touch, feeling his body ready for danger—the more easily these sensory pieces broke through.

Because those intrusions felt unbearable and almost impossible to speak about, Rafael began managing them the only ways he could think of. He tried hard not to think about the crash at all, cutting off conversations and mentally shoving images away the instant they began. At night he stayed up very late, lingering over television or sitting awake in the dark because sleep felt too unguarded and because closing his eyes made the sounds more likely to come. Sometimes, when the memory pressed in, he deliberately tried to blank out and “go somewhere else,” describing it as leaving his body just enough not to feel the full force of it. These strategies gave him brief relief, but they also seemed to leave the event even less put into words; what remained were the same raw sounds, the same unspeakable fragments, and the same shame each time they returned.

Over time, these habits changed how Rafael understood himself. Because he was avoiding the memory rather than making sense of it, he became more convinced that something in him had been permanently altered. He had come to believe he would never feel normal emotions again, only some mixture of fear, anger, and deadness. When he found himself staying up half the night or mentally disappearing in the middle of distress, he took this not as a sign of struggle but as evidence of damage: proof, in his mind, that he was weak, defective, the sort of man to whom terrible things happen and who cannot stop them. The very methods he used to get through the day deepened his bleak view of himself.

That view, in turn, kept the sense of threat close. If he was inherently vulnerable and the world fundamentally uncontrollable, then of course he needed to watch every doorway and keep his body ready. In class he has become more distant with students, stepping out of partnering demonstrations when possible and positioning himself near the studio exit. His wife has noticed he lingers awake long after she has gone to bed and seems elsewhere when she asks about the accident. Rafael finally sought help after startling so intensely when a younger dancer adjusted his arm from behind that he shouted and stopped rehearsal cold. What frightened him most was not only the reaction itself, but the conviction that this was now his permanent self: a man who cannot speak the worst thing that happened to him, cannot trust safety when it is present, and may never feel like himself again. He says he is coming now because he wants, more than anything, to know whether the crash still has to live in his body this way.
